claim: Ndst1 was one of the most robustly and significantly up-regulated genes after demyelination in purified oligodendroglia from adult demyelinated animals compared to healthy animals.
source: One of the most robustly and significantly up-regulated genes after demyelination was Ndst1, a key enzyme of HS proteoglycan synthesis (fold increase of 48.9 and 14.0 in two different trials; p≤0.001; microarray data are available at GEO with accession number GSE47486).
evidence: Supported by microarray data showing fold increases of 48.9 and 14.0 in two trials with p≤0.001

claim: Ndst1 was highly expressed by Olig2+ cells after EAE in the corpus callosum in close proximity to lesion sites.
source: This up-regulation of Ndst1 was confirmed in vivo at 21 days in mice exposed to EAE by in situ hybridization combined with Olig2 labeling, a pan OLG marker. While Ndst1 was not detected in the corpus callosum of control brains (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), it was highly expressed by the Olig2+ population after EAE in the corpus callosum (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C) in close proximity to lesion sites (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data combined with Olig2 labeling shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: Ndst1 expression levels increased by a mean of 41% in the demyelinated corpus callosum compared to healthy corpus callosum at 8 days post injection.
source: We quantified a mean 41% increase in the Ndst1 expression level in the demyelinated corpus callosum compared to healthy corpus callosum (Figure 1B; p=0.05).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR analysis shown in Figure 1B with p=0.05

claim: Ndst1 expressing cells delimited a belt around the lesion site at 5 and 8 days post injection.
source: At days 5 and 8 dpi, Ndst1 expressing cells delimited a belt around the lesion site.
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization observations at multiple time points

claim: N-sulfated HS positive puncta formed a belt around the demyelination lesion, similar to the profile of Ndst1-induction.
source: While no staining was detected in the contralateral corpus callosum (Figure 2A), N-sulfated HS positive puncta formed a belt around the demyelination lesion (Figure 2B–C), similar to the profile of Ndst1-induction.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining with 10E4 antibody shown in Figure 2

claim: The 10E4 antibody exclusively detects N-sulfated motifs produced by Ndst1 activity.
source: To do so, we used the anti-HS antibody 10E4 (Grobe, 2005; Pan et al., 2014), which exclusively detects the N-sulfated motifs produced by Ndst1 activity (Pallerla et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Grobe, 2005; Pan et al., 2014; Pallerla et al., 2007)

claim: The HS staining with 10E4 antibody was absent after treatment with Heparinase.
source: This staining is specific as it was absent after treatment with Heparinase, an enzyme that digests N-sulfated motifs on the HS chains (David et al., 1992; Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by experimental control shown in Figure 2D and cited reference (David et al., 1992)

claim: 98.0 ± 1.5% of Ndst1+ cells express Olig2, indicating that virtually all Ndst1 cells belong to the oligodendroglia lineage.
source: We quantified that 98.0 ± 1.5% Ndst1+ cells express Olig2 indicating that virtually all Nsdt1 cells belong to the oligodendroglia lineage (Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by quantification of co-labeling experiments

claim: At 5 days post injection, 97.5 ± 1.7% of Ndst1 expressing cells were co-labeled with CC1, a mature oligodendrocyte marker.
source: At five dpi, 97.5 ± 1.7% of Ndst1 expressing cells were co-labeled with CC1, a mature OLG marker (Figure 3D)
evidence: Supported by quantification of immunostaining shown in Figure 3D

claim: At 5 days post injection, only 0.8 ± 0.3% of Ndst1 expressing cells co-expressed the OPC marker PDGFRα.
source: while only 0.8 ± 0.3% co-expressed the OPC marker PDGFRα (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by quantification of immunostaining shown in Figure 3C

claim: Only half (45.8 ± 3.4%) of the Olig2+ cells in the belt surrounding the lesion expressed Ndst1.
source: Of note, in the belt delimitated by Ndst1 staining surrounding the lesion, only half of the Olig2+ cells expressed Ndst1 (45.8 ± 3.4%).
evidence: Supported by quantification of co-labeling

claim: 8.5 ± 3.2% of PDGFRα+ cells surrounding the lesion co-labeled with Ndst1.
source: We observed that, 8.5 ± 3.2% of PDGFRα+ cells and 48.9 ± 8.5% of CC1+ cells surrounding the lesion co-labeled with Ndst1.
evidence: Supported by quantification of co-labeling experiments

claim: 48.9 ± 8.5% of CC1+ cells surrounding the lesion co-labeled with Ndst1.
source: We observed that, 8.5 ± 3.2% of PDGFRα+ cells and 48.9 ± 8.5% of CC1+ cells surrounding the lesion co-labeled with Ndst1.
evidence: Supported by quantification of co-labeling experiments

claim: The majority of Ndst1+ cells around the lesion are mature oligodendrocytes which are more prone than OPC to activate Ndst1 expression in response to demyelination.
source: Our data indicate that the majority of Ndst1+ cells around the lesion are mature OLG which are more prone than OPC to activate Ndst1 expression in response to demyelination.
evidence: Inferred from the quantification data showing 97.5% of Ndst1+ cells are CC1+ while only 0.8% are PDGFRα+

claim: A significant reduction of 53% in N-sulfated HS positive puncta around the demyelination lesion was observed in Olig2-Cre+/-; Ndst1 Flox/Flox mutant mice compared to control.
source: As revealed by immunostaining using the anti-HS antibody, a significant reduction of 53% of the staining in N-sulfated HS positive puncta around the demyelination lesion was also observed in mutant compared to control (Figure 4G–I; p=0.05).
evidence: Supported by quantification of immunostaining shown in Figure 4G-I with p=0.05

claim: Conditional deletion of Ndst1 in the Olig2+ cell population does not interfere with brain development and subsequent myelin maturation in healthy adult mice.
source: In healthy mice, quantitative analysis of myelin content (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C; p=0.2), astrocyte density (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–F; p=0.4) and oligodendroglial lineage cell density (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G–L; p=0.6, 0.2 and 0.2 for Olig2, CC1 and PDGFRα cell density respectively) revealed no difference between control (Olig2-Cre+/-) and mutant (Olig2-Cre+/-; Ndst1 Flox/Flox) adult mice, thus indicating that conditional deletion of Ndst1 in the Olig2+ cell population does not interfere with brain development and with subsequent myelin maturation.
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 with no significant differences

claim: No difference in lesion size was detected between control and mutant mice at 4 days post injection.
source: While no difference was detected at four dpi (0.226 ± 0.036 vs. 0.159±0.033 mm³ in control and mutant mice, respectively; p=0.23)
evidence: Supported by lesion size measurements with p=0.23

claim: A significant two-fold increase in lesion size was observed in Ndst1 mutant mice compared to control mice at 8 days post injection.
source: a significant two-fold increase in lesion size was observed in mutant compared to control mice at eight dpi (0.199 ± 0.032 vs. 0.097±0.022 mm³, p=0.023) (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: Supported by lesion size measurements shown in Figure 5A-C with p=0.023

claim: Lesion sizes reached comparable values in control and mutant mice at 14 days post injection.
source: During the remyelination phase (between 8 and 14 dpi), the lesion area decreased in both groups reaching comparable sizes at 14 dpi (0.033 ± 0.02 vs. 0.028±0.012 mm³ in control and mutant mice, respectively; p=0.97) (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by lesion size measurements shown in Figure 5C with p=0.97

claim: There was a marked decrease in Olig2+ cell density within the demyelinated area compared to healthy corpus callosum in both control and mutant groups at 4 days post injection.
source: In accordance with demyelination, there was a marked decrease in Olig2+ cell density within the demyelinated area compared to healthy corpus callosum in both groups at four dpi (55.5 ± 3.3% and 57.3 ± 3.9% decrease in control and mutant mice respectively, p=0.03 and p=0.001) (Figure 5F)
evidence: Supported by quantification shown in Figure 5F with p=0.03 and p=0.001

claim: The density of Olig2+ cells returned to uninjected control values at 14 days post injection in both control and mutant mice.
source: We observe that in both conditions the density of Olig2+ cells returned to uninjected control values at 14 dpi.
evidence: Supported by quantification of Olig2+ cell density over time

claim: Cell differentiation is not affected by Ndst1 inactivation as indicated by no significant difference in mature oligodendrocyte (CC1+) density between control and mutant mice.
source: Quantification of mean cell densities of mature OLG (CC1+) (Figure 5G–I) within the lesion throughout the time course revealed no significant difference between the two groups indicating that cell differentiation is not affected by Ndst1 inactivation.
evidence: Supported by quantification shown in Figure 5G-I showing no significant differences

claim: The density of Ki67+ proliferating cells within the lesion area was two-fold increased in Ndst1 mutant mice compared to control mice at 8 days post injection.
source: We observed that the density of Ki67+ proliferating cells within the lesion area was two-fold increased in Ndst1 mutant mice compared to control mice at eight dpi (217.8 ± 42.8% vs. 100±13.5% in mutant and control mice, respectively, p=0.037) (Figure 5J–K).
evidence: Supported by quantification shown in Figure 5J-K with p=0.037

claim: The percentage of proliferating Olig2+ cells was significantly increased in mutant mice at 8 days post injection.
source: At eight dpi, the percentage of proliferating Olig2+ cells was significantly increased in mutant mice (7.6 ± 0.8% vs 3.2 ± 0.5% in mutant and control mice, respectively, p=0.0004) indicating a prolongation of OPC reactivity during the repair phase.
evidence: Supported by quantification with p=0.0004

claim: No significant difference in cell death was detectable in the lesion between control and mutant groups at 4 days post injection.
source: To note, no significant difference in cell death was detectable in the lesion between the two groups at four dpi (341.7 ± 4.5 and 357 ± 111.1 caspase3+ cells per mm² in control and mutant mice, respectively, p=0.28).
evidence: Supported by quantification of caspase3+ cells with p=0.28

claim: Ndst1 expression in the Olig2+ population has no effect on initial demyelination but protects the lesion from enlarging and participates in the control of OPC mobilization.
source: Together, these results suggest that Ndst1 expression in the Olig2+ population has no effect on initial demyelination (equivalent lesion size at four dpi) but protects the lesion from enlarging and participates in the control of OPC mobilization.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of equivalent lesion sizes at 4 dpi but increased lesion size at 8 dpi in mutants, and altered OPC proliferation

claim: There was a robust increase in proliferation of CD68+ cells in mutant mice compared to control mice at 8 days post injection.
source: We found a robust increase in proliferation of CD68+ cells in mutant compared to control mice at eight dpi (166.4 ± 24.3 vs. 79.3 ± 20.6 CD68+/Ki67+ cells per mm² in mutant and control mice, respectively, p=0.026) (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: Supported by quantification shown in Figure 6A-C with p=0.026

claim: There was a switch of microglia/macrophage polarization in favor of the rhomboid phenotype in mutant mice compared to control at 8 days post injection.
source: We observed a switch of the microglia/macrophage polarization among the whole Iba1 and CD68 population in favor of the rhomboid phenotype in mutant mice compared to control at eight dpi. This effect was quantified for activated microglia (ratio of rhomboid/ramified CD68+ cells of 0.28 ± 0.05 in control vs. 0.66 ± 0.1 in mutant mice, p=0.038) (Figure 6H).
evidence: Supported by quantification shown in Figure 6H with p=0.038

claim: There was a significant 77% increase in the number of Cox2+ microglial cells in mutant mice compared to control, indicating a delay in the M1 to M2 switch.
source: We then evaluated the expression level of Cox2, a marker of pro-inflammatory (M1) microglia/macrophage (Chhor et al., 2017) and observed a significant 77% increase in the number of Cox2+ microglial cells in mutant mice compared to control (p=0.01), indicating a delay in the pro-inflammatory (M1) to pro-regenerative (M2) switch in the absence of Ndst1 in oligodendroglia (Figure 6I–K).
evidence: Supported by quantification shown in Figure 6I-K with p=0.01 and citation (Chhor et al., 2017)

claim: Ndst1 deletion in the Olig2 population is sufficient to enhance microglia/macrophage proliferation and activation at the lesion site at the onset of remyelination.
source: These results demonstrate that Ndst1 deletion in the Olig2 population is sufficient to enhance microglia/macrophage proliferation and activation at the lesion site at the onset of remyelination.
evidence: Inferred from the data showing increased CD68+ cell proliferation, rhomboid polarization, and Cox2 expression in mutants

claim: AP-Shh binding delimited a clear belt surrounding the lesion site in the corpus callosum after LPC injection.
source: While no AP-Shh binding was observed in healthy or uninjured contralateral corpus callosum, AP-Shh binding delimited a clear belt surrounding the lesion site in the corpus callosum after LPC injection (Figure 7B–B').
evidence: Supported by AP-Shh binding assay shown in Figure 7B-B'

claim: AP-Shh-CWdeleted did not bind around the lesion on adjacent sections.
source: In contrast, AP-Shh-CWdeleted did not bind around the same lesion on adjacent sections (Figure 7C–D).
evidence: Supported by AP-Shh-CWdeleted binding assay shown in Figure 7C-D

claim: Endogenous Shh localization and concentration may be controlled by HS production by peri-lesional oligodendrocytes.
source: As AP-Shh binding depends on the integrity of its HS-binding motif, this indicates that endogenous Shh localization and concentration may be controlled by HS production by peri-lesional OLG.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that AP-Shh binds around lesions while AP-Shh-CWdeleted does not

claim: Ndst1 mutant mice exhibited 38% decrease in Ptch1 expression compared to control mice at 8 days post injection, although it did not quite reach significance.
source: Ndst1 mutant mice exhibited 38% decrease in Ptch1 expression compared to control mice (8.6 ± 0.7 vs 13.8 ± 3.0 dots/cells in mutant and control mice respectively, n = 5 mice/group) although it did not quite reach significance (p=0.07) (Figure 7E).
evidence: Supported by RNAscope quantification shown in Figure 7E with p=0.07

claim: Lack of NDST1 in oligodendrocyte lineage attenuates SHH signaling following demyelination insult.
source: Altogether these results suggest that lack of NDST1 in OLG lineage attenuates SHH signaling following demyelination insult.
evidence: Inferred from the reduced Ptch1 expression in mutant mice

claim: There is a trend to increased Ndst1 expression in oligodendrocytes in MS tissue compared to control tissue based on snRNAseq data.
source: We first probed the snRNAseq data provided by Jakel et al work (Jäkel et al., 2019), and observed that few cells express Ndst1 in both control and MS tissues but when the oligodendrocytes that express Ndst1 are compared, there is a trend to increased expression in MS tissue (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by analysis of snRNAseq data from Jäkel et al., 2019 shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1

claim: There was a significant increase of NDST1 labeling in MS patients white matter compared to control white matter without MS.
source: While NDST1 staining was very weak in control WM (without MS), we observed a significant increase of NDST1 labeling in MS patients WM (Figure 8A–B).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining shown in Figure 8A-B

claim: There is a significant increase of NDST1 staining in multiple sclerosis lesions compared to control.
source: Comparison of healthy control, MS normal appearing WM and MS lesions showed that there is a significant increase of NDST1 staining in multiple sclerosis lesions vs. control (p=0.0014) (Figure 8C).
evidence: Supported by quantification shown in Figure 8C with p=0.0014

claim: There is significantly more NDST1 labeling in MS lesions compared to their surrounding normal appearing white matter.
source: Comparison of each MS lesion with its surrounding normal appearing WM using a paired t test, revealed that there is significantly more NDST1 labeling in MS lesions compared to their surrounding normal appearing WM (paired two-tailed t test, t9 = 3.39, p=0.0095).
evidence: Supported by paired t-test with t9 = 3.39, p=0.0095

claim: NDST1+ cells were distributed evenly throughout MS lesions, rather than forming a delimiting band.
source: However, NDST1+ cells were distributed evenly throughout the lesion, rather than forming a delimiting band (Figure 8—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Supported by observation shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2D

claim: The majority of NDST1 cells in MS lesions and normal appearing white matter were oligodendroglia.
source: Quantitative analysis showed that the majority of NDST1 cells were oligodendroglia in all types of lesions (remyelinated, active, chronic active, chronic inactive) and in normal appearing WM (Figure 8H).
evidence: Supported by quantification of double-labeling shown in Figure 8H

claim: The vast majority of OLIG2+ cells in MS lesions expressed NDST1, with a gradual reduction in the proportion of OLIG2+NDST1+ cells as lesions become more chronic.
source: The vast majority of OLIG2+ cells in the lesions expressed NDST1, with a gradual reduction in the proportion of OLIG2+NDST1+ cells as lesions become more chronic, and with significantly fewer in control tissue (Figure 8I; p=0.016).
evidence: Supported by quantification shown in Figure 8I with p=0.016

claim: The number of NDST1+ oligodendroglia in each MS lesion was inversely correlated with the lesion's size.
source: The number of NDST1+ oligodendroglia in each lesion was inversely correlated with the lesion's size (Figure 8J).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 8J

claim: NDST1+ cell density positively correlated with patient's score of remyelination ability.
source: We showed that NDST1+ cell density positively correlated with patient's score of remyelination ability (Figure 8K).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 8K

claim: MS tissues with a higher repair potential display a high number of NDST1+ cells, suggesting that higher numbers of NDST1+ cells in a lesion may provide a positive environmental support for myelin repair.
source: These data reveal that MS tissues with a higher repair potential (containing most active and remyelinated lesions) display a high number of NDST1+ cells therefore suggesting that higher numbers of NDST1+ cells in a lesion may provide a positive environmental support for myelin repair.
evidence: Inferred from the positive correlation between NDST1+ cell density and remyelination score

claim: Ndst1 is almost exclusively expressed by oligodendroglia present at the margin of the lesion delimiting the lesion from the intact corpus callosum.
source: First, we show that Ndst1 is almost exclusively expressed by oligodendroglia present at the margin of the lesion delimiting the lesion from the intact corpus callosum.
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization and immunostaining data showing Ndst1 expression pattern and co-localization with oligodendrocyte markers

claim: Conditional deletion of Ndst1 in the Olig2 population triggers an enlargement of the LPC-induced demyelinated area.
source: Second, we found that the conditional deletion of Ndst1 in the Olig2 population concomitantly triggers an enlargement of the LPC-induced demyelinated area, alters OPC mobilization and favors the pro-inflammatory (M1) phenotype in microglia.
evidence: Supported by lesion size measurements and cell phenotype analyses in mutant mice

claim: Conditional deletion of Ndst1 in the Olig2 population alters OPC mobilization.
source: Second, we found that the conditional deletion of Ndst1 in the Olig2 population concomitantly triggers an enlargement of the LPC-induced demyelinated area, alters OPC mobilization and favors the pro-inflammatory (M1) phenotype in microglia.
evidence: Supported by OPC proliferation data in mutant mice

claim: Conditional deletion of Ndst1 in the Olig2 population favors the pro-inflammatory (M1) phenotype in microglia.
source: Second, we found that the conditional deletion of Ndst1 in the Olig2 population concomitantly triggers an enlargement of the LPC-induced demyelinated area, alters OPC mobilization and favors the pro-inflammatory (M1) phenotype in microglia.
evidence: Supported by Cox2 expression and microglia polarization data in mutant mice

claim: The effects of Ndst1 deletion could be mediated through HS dependent binding of the morphogen Shh.
source: We propose that these effects could be mediated through HS dependent binding of the morphogen Shh which has been shown to be a positive regulator of myelin repair through increased oligodendrogenesis and microglial regulation (Ferent et al., 2013; Zakaria et al., 2019).
evidence: Speculative mechanism based on AP-Shh binding data and citations to previous studies (Ferent et al., 2013; Zakaria et al., 2019)

claim: NDST1 is up-regulated in MS brain tissue samples, especially within lesions.
source: Finally, using MS brain tissue samples, we show that NDST1 is up-regulated, especially within lesions and that the density of NDST1+ cells in these lesions is negatively correlated to lesion size, and positively correlated to the patient's potential remyelination ability.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and quantification in human MS tissue

claim: The density of NDST1+ cells in MS lesions is negatively correlated to lesion size.
source: Finally, using MS brain tissue samples, we show that NDST1 is up-regulated, especially within lesions and that the density of NDST1+ cells in these lesions is negatively correlated to lesion size, and positively correlated to the patient's potential remyelination ability.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis in human MS tissue

claim: The density of NDST1+ cells in MS lesions is positively correlated to the patient's potential remyelination ability.
source: Finally, using MS brain tissue samples, we show that NDST1 is up-regulated, especially within lesions and that the density of NDST1+ cells in these lesions is negatively correlated to lesion size, and positively correlated to the patient's potential remyelination ability.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis in human MS tissue

claim: Ndst1/HS expressed by oligodendrocytes around the lesion create a protective and permissive environment playing a positive role in myelin repair.
source: Our data suggest that Ndst1/HS expressed by oligodendrocytes around the lesion create a protective and permissive environment playing a positive role in myelin repair.
evidence: Inferred from the combined mouse and human data showing protective effects of Ndst1/HS

claim: Chondroitin sulfates are strongly expressed by astrocytes and microglia providing a hostile environment impeding regeneration and remyelination following brain injury.
source: Chondroitin sulfates are strongly expressed by astrocytes and microglia providing a hostile environment impeding regeneration and remyelination following brain injury (Siebert and Osterhout, 2011; Pendleton et al., 2013; Deng et al., 2015; Lau et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Siebert and Osterhout, 2011; Pendleton et al., 2013; Deng et al., 2015; Lau et al., 2012)

claim: Enzymatic degradation of chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans using chondroïtinase ABC treatment in vivo promotes OPC mobilization and remyelination.
source: Enzymatic degradation of chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans using chondroïtinase ABC treatment in vivo promotes OPC mobilization and remyelination (Lau et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Lau et al., 2012)

claim: In vitro, chondroitin sulfates reduce OPC maturation.
source: In vitro, chondroitin sulfates reduce OPC maturation (Karus et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Karus et al., 2016)

claim: The use of a CSPG synthesis inhibitor promotes OPC maturation and accelerates remyelination following focal demyelination in mice.
source: and in vivo the use of a CSPG synthesis inhibitor promotes OPC maturation and accelerates remyelination following focal demyelination in mice (Keough et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Keough et al., 2016)

claim: Surfen, a proteoglycan binding agent, reduces inflammation and delays remyelination.
source: A recent study has shown that Surfen, a proteoglycan binding agent, reduces inflammation and delays remyelination. (Warford et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Warford et al., 2018)

claim: Two classes of sulfated proteoglycans have opposite effects on myelin repair; chondroitin sulfates being detrimental and HS having a beneficial effect.
source: Therefore, two classes of sulfated proteoglycans have opposite effects on myelin repair; one being detrimental (chondroitin sulfates), and the other (HS) having a beneficial effect.
evidence: Inferred from the comparison of effects of chondroitin sulfates and HS on remyelination

claim: Pre-existing mature oligodendrocytes can participate in myelin regeneration in human and rodent by forming new myelin sheaths.
source: Interesting, recent data have shown that pre-existing mature OLG can also participate to myelin regeneration in human and rodent by forming new myelin sheaths further indicating that mature OLG have an active role in myelin repair (Yeung et al., 2019; Duncan et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Yeung et al., 2019; Duncan et al., 2018)

claim: Efficient remyelination requires the dynamic regulation of functional microglia phenotype.
source: Recent studies have shown that efficient remyelination required the dynamic regulation of functional microglia phenotype (Miron et al., 2013; Lloyd et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Miron et al., 2013; Lloyd et al., 2019)

claim: Microglia respond to demyelination with initial pro-inflammatory phenotype (M1) followed later by pro-regenerative phenotype (M2) which actively contributes to myelin repair.
source: Microglia respond to demyelination with initial pro-inflammatory phenotype (M1) followed later by pro-regenerative phenotype (M2) which actively contributes to myelin repair (Miron et al., 2013; Olah et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Miron et al., 2013; Olah et al., 2012)

claim: The transition from pro-inflammatory to pro-regenerative microglia phenotype is a rate-limiting step in the repair process.
source: Interestingly, this transition from pro-inflammatory to pro-regenerative phenotype is a rate-limiting step in the repair process since intra-lesional depletion of pro-regenerative microglia blocks oligodendrocyte differentiation and delays the regenerative process (Miron et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Miron et al., 2013)

claim: Intra-lesional depletion of pro-regenerative microglia blocks oligodendrocyte differentiation and delays the regenerative process.
source: Interestingly, this transition from pro-inflammatory to pro-regenerative phenotype is a rate-limiting step in the repair process since intra-lesional depletion of pro-regenerative microglia blocks oligodendrocyte differentiation and delays the regenerative process (Miron et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Miron et al., 2013)

claim: Ndst1 global knock out mice display developmental defects that mainly resemble those found in embryos deficient for Shh or FGFs.
source: Ndst1 global knock out mice display developmental defects that mainly resemble those found in embryos deficient for Shh or FGFs (Pallerla et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Pallerla et al., 2008)

claim: FGF signaling is not required for myelin regeneration in acute models of demyelination including LPC-induced demyelination of the spinal cord and cuprizone intoxication.
source: This study revealed that FGF signaling is not required for myelin regeneration in acute models of demyelination including LPC-induced demyelination of the spinal cord and cuprizone intoxication (Furusho et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Furusho et al., 2015)

claim: Blocking Shh activity leads to an increase in demyelinated lesion size and an altered OPC mobilization after LPC-induced demyelination.
source: By contrast, blocking Shh activity leads to an increase in demyelinated lesion size and an altered OPC mobilization after LPC-induced demyelination (Ferent et al., 2013) similar to what we observe in Olig2-Cre; Ndst1 Flox/Flox mice.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Ferent et al., 2013)

claim: The proteolytic processing of Shh required for signaling pathway activation is finely regulated by HS chains.
source: Of note, recent in vitro findings show that the proteolytic processing of Shh required for signaling pathway activation (Ohlig et al., 2012) is finely regulated by HS chains (Ortmann et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Ohlig et al., 2012; Ortmann et al., 2015)

claim: The main Shh responding cells after LPC-induced demyelination of the corpus callosum are oligodendrocytes and microglia.
source: Interestingly, Ferent et al., 2013 have shown that the main Shh responding cells (cells expressing Gli1 and/or Smo) after LPC-induced demyelination of the corpus callosum are OLG and microglia.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Ferent et al., 2013)

claim: High levels of HS proteoglycans and chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans have been previously associated with inflammatory CNS diseases such as MS.
source: High levels of HS proteoglycans and chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans have been previously associated with inflammatory CNS diseases such as MS (Briani et al., 2002; Berezin et al., 2014; van Horssen et al., 2006; Satoh et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Briani et al., 2002; Berezin et al., 2014; van Horssen et al., 2006; Satoh et al., 2009)

claim: NDST1 expression is significantly higher in MS lesions compared to surrounding normal appearing white matter, irrespective of lesion type.
source: NDST1 expression is significantly higher in MS lesions compared to surrounding normal appearing white matter (NAWM), irrespective of lesion type (remyelinated, active, chronic active or chronic inactive).
evidence: Supported by quantification in human MS tissue

claim: Mature oligodendrocytes surrounding demyelinated lesions are not passive witnesses but contribute to protection and regeneration by producing HS.
source: Our study suggests that mature OLG surrounding demyelinated lesions are not passive witnesses but contribute to protection and regeneration by producing HS.
evidence: Inferred from the combined data showing Ndst1 expression in mature OLG and protective effects of HS

claim: Myelin loss remains in defined areas rather than expanding to involve all of the white matter in multiple sclerosis.
source: Myelin loss remains in defined areas, rather than expanding to involve all of the white matter, and the mechanism by which demyelinated lesions stop expanding is not understood.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about MS pathology

claim: The mechanism by which demyelinated lesions stop expanding is not understood.
source: Myelin loss remains in defined areas, rather than expanding to involve all of the white matter, and the mechanism by which demyelinated lesions stop expanding is not understood.
evidence: Statement of current knowledge gap

claim: Remyelination involves OPC recruitment to the lesion, differentiation into myelin forming cells and remyelination of denuded axons.
source: Remyelination involves OPC recruitment to the lesion, differentiation into myelin forming cells and remyelination of denuded axons, and the success of this depends on environmental context, including secreted factors from neighboring cells (Franklin and Ffrench-Constant, 2008; Patrikios et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Franklin and Ffrench-Constant, 2008; Patrikios et al., 2006)

claim: The success of remyelination depends on environmental context, including secreted factors from neighboring cells.
source: Remyelination involves OPC recruitment to the lesion, differentiation into myelin forming cells and remyelination of denuded axons, and the success of this depends on environmental context, including secreted factors from neighboring cells (Franklin and Ffrench-Constant, 2008; Patrikios et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Franklin and Ffrench-Constant, 2008; Patrikios et al., 2006)

claim: The repair process of remyelination occurs spontaneously in MS patients and is highly variable between patients and between lesions.
source: This repair process, which occurs spontaneously in MS patients, is highly variable between patients and between lesions (Patrikios et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Patrikios et al., 2006)

claim: Regenerative failure in MS is mainly attributed to defects in OPC recruitment towards the demyelinated areas.
source: Regenerative failure is mainly attributed to defects in OPC recruitment towards the demyelinated areas (Boyd et al., 2013) and/or to their incapacity to differentiate into myelinating OLG at the lesion site (Franklin and Ffrench-Constant, 2008; Wolswijk, 1998; Chang et al., 2002; Franklin, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Boyd et al., 2013; Franklin and Ffrench-Constant, 2008; Wolswijk, 1998; Chang et al., 2002; Franklin, 2002)

claim: Regenerative failure in MS is attributed to OPC incapacity to differentiate into myelinating oligodendrocytes at the lesion site.
source: Regenerative failure is mainly attributed to defects in OPC recruitment towards the demyelinated areas (Boyd et al., 2013) and/or to their incapacity to differentiate into myelinating OLG at the lesion site (Franklin and Ffrench-Constant, 2008; Wolswijk, 1998; Chang et al., 2002; Franklin, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Franklin and Ffrench-Constant, 2008; Wolswijk, 1998; Chang et al., 2002; Franklin, 2002)

claim: Reactive astrocytes or microglia and macrophages produce multiple factors involved in the regenerative process.
source: Multiple factors are involved in this regenerative process including those produced by reactive astrocytes or microglia and macrophages (Miron et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Miron et al., 2013)

claim: Reactive astrocytes and microglia/macrophages contribute to myelin destruction but also to myelin debris removal and beneficial effects by secreting factors that support remyelination.
source: These contribute to myelin destruction, but also to myelin debris removal and beneficial effects by secreting factors that directly or indirectly support remyelination (El Waly et al., 2014; Emery, 2010; Aguirre et al., 2007; Williams et al., 2007; Courtès et al., 2011; Vernerey et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (El Waly et al., 2014; Emery, 2010; Aguirre et al., 2007; Williams et al., 2007; Courtès et al., 2011; Vernerey et al., 2013)

claim: Oligodendrocyte lineage cells produce factors that modulate remyelination, such as the morphogen Shh.
source: Interestingly oligodendrocyte lineage cells also produce factors that modulate remyelination, such as the morphogen shh which is produced by OLG and OPC at the onset of demyelination in lysophosphatidyl choline (LPC)-induced lesions (Ferent et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Ferent et al., 2013)

claim: Shh is produced by oligodendrocytes and OPC at the onset of demyelination in LPC-induced lesions.
source: Interestingly oligodendrocyte lineage cells also produce factors that modulate remyelination, such as the morphogen shh which is produced by OLG and OPC at the onset of demyelination in lysophosphatidyl choline (LPC)-induced lesions (Ferent et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Ferent et al., 2013)

claim: Blocking Shh activity induces an increase in lesion size and a block in OPC proliferation and differentiation.
source: In this context, blocking Shh activity induces an increase in lesion size and a block in OPC proliferation and differentiation, and conversely Shh overexpression leads to the attenuation of the lesion extent and promotes oligodendrogenesis (Ferent et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Ferent et al., 2013)

claim: Shh overexpression leads to the attenuation of the lesion extent and promotes oligodendrogenesis.
source: In this context, blocking Shh activity induces an increase in lesion size and a block in OPC proliferation and differentiation, and conversely Shh overexpression leads to the attenuation of the lesion extent and promotes oligodendrogenesis (Ferent et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Ferent et al., 2013)

claim: HSPGs play a critical role in regulating spatiotemporal coordination of signals in the extracellular microenvironment during brain development and in adulthood.
source: One of these key factors may be HS proteoglycans (HSPG), as there is now compelling evidence that HSPGs play a critical role in regulating spatiotemporal coordination of signals in the extracellular microenvironment of many tissues during brain development and in adulthood (Sarrazin et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Sarrazin et al., 2011)

claim: Ndst enzymes perform the first step of sugar modifications thus specifying the functional properties of HSPGs.
source: Ndst enzymes perform the first step of these sugar modifications thus specifying the functional properties of HSPGs (Lindahl et al., 1998; Perrimon and Bernfield, 2000; Carlsson et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Lindahl et al., 1998; Perrimon and Bernfield, 2000; Carlsson et al., 2008)

claim: Ndst1 appears as the key enzyme for addition of N-sulfated motifs to HS chains in brain during development.
source: Among the four known Ndst enzymes, Ndst1 appears as the key enzyme for addition of N-sulfated motifs to HS chains in brain during development, as shown by limited functional redundancy mediated by other Ndst enzymes (2-4) in Ndst1 KO mice (Grobe, 2005; Pallerla et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Grobe, 2005; Pallerla et al., 2007)

claim: During development, HS proteoglycans provide an important signaling scaffold allowing spatial concentration or trapping of numerous molecules such as morphogens and growth factors.
source: During development, HS proteoglycans provide an important signaling scaffold allowing spatial concentration or trapping of numerous molecules such as morphogens and growth factors (Matsuo and Kimura-Yoshida, 2014) and the control of receptor activity (Matsuo and Kimura-Yoshida, 2014; Gallagher, 2001; Häcker et al., 2005; Parker and Kohler, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Matsuo and Kimura-Yoshida, 2014; Gallagher, 2001; Häcker et al., 2005; Parker and Kohler, 2010)

claim: Following CNS injury, HSPGs play a pivotal role in post-lesional plasticity and regeneration.
source: Following CNS injury, HSPGs are known to play a pivotal role in post-lesional plasticity and regeneration (Iseki et al., 2002; Hagino et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Iseki et al., 2002; Hagino et al., 2003)

claim: Some HS proteoglycans are over-expressed by reactive astrocytes in injured mouse brain.
source: Some HS proteoglycans are over-expressed by reactive astrocytes in injured mouse brain and provide positive (Iseki et al., 2002) or negative (Hagino et al., 2003) environmental support for axon regenerative responses.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Iseki et al., 2002; Hagino et al., 2003)

claim: In vitro, HS proteoglycans can prevent oligodendrocyte differentiation, maintaining OPC in an immature proliferative phenotype by acting as a FGF-2 co-receptor.
source: In vitro, HS proteoglycans can prevent OLG differentiation, maintaining OPC in an immature proliferative phenotype by acting as a FGF-2 co-receptor (McKinnon et al., 1990; Bansal and Pfeiffer, 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (McKinnon et al., 1990; Bansal and Pfeiffer, 1997)

claim: In the LPC model, demyelination occurs within few days, endogenous progenitor mobilization peaks at eight days post injection and is followed by OPC differentiation.
source: In this model, demyelination is not T cell driven, and demyelination and remyelination proceed in a stereotypic sequence: demyelination occurs within few days, endogenous progenitor mobilization peaks at eight dpi and is followed by OPC differentiation (El Waly et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (El Waly et al., 2014)

claim: Production of new myelin is observed after 2 weeks in the LPC model.
source: Production of new myelin is then observed after 2 weeks.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of the LPC model timeline

claim: The lesion in the LPC model is characterized by a strong increase in cell density due to glia proliferation and microglia/macrophage infiltration.
source: The lesion is also characterized by a strong increase in cell density (due to glia proliferation and to microglia/macrophage infiltration) observed by Hoechst staining (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) that strictly coincides with loss of GFP fluorescence.
evidence: Supported by observation shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2
